title: the prayer you know by heart
hook: the prayer you can say start to finish, and what it asks for
carry: a prayer for a clear mind

segments.voice: Yesterday: om, three sounds and a silence. Today it opens a prayer you might already know by heart.

Om bhur bhuvah svah. If you grew up in a Hindu home, there's a good chance you can say the rest without thinking. Maybe someone said it every morning. Maybe it played at every puja. Now the hard part: what does it mean? Most people go quiet. Today, line by line. First, a guess.
screen: `OM BHUR BHUVAH SVAH…` → `YOU CAN SAY IT.` → `WHAT DOES IT MEAN?`

segments.voice: It's called the Gayatri mantra, and it's one of the oldest verses Hindus still say every day. Take it a line at a time. Om: the sound from yesterday. Bhur bhuvah svah: earth, sky, and everything beyond: the whole world. Tat savitur varenyam: that bright, worthy light of the sun. Bhargo devasya dhimahi: we meditate on that divine radiance. Dhiyo yo nah prachodayat: may it wake up and guide our minds. Notice what it asks for. Not money. Not luck. Not to win. A clear mind. That's what a mantra is: the word comes from man, to think, and tra, a tool. A tool for the mind, said on purpose. Many families say the Gayatri at dawn, as the light comes up, and some say it a set number of times on beads. Once you know the lines, it stops being a sound you repeat and becomes a request you mean.
screen: `OM — THE SOUND FROM YESTERDAY.` · `EARTH, SKY, AND BEYOND.` · `MAY IT WAKE UP OUR MINDS.` · `A TOOL FOR THE MIND.`

segments.voice: One breath with the bell. Breathe in. As you breathe out, say the Gayatri once, slowly, out loud or in your head, or just its last line: dhiyo yo nah prachodayat, may it wake up and guide our minds. This time, mean the words.
Gayatri. The morning prayer for a clear mind, and a mantra: a tool for the mind. Third word on your strand.
Your line: a prayer for a clear mind. Next time you hear it, you'll know what's being asked. Day three.

story.title: the king who wanted to be a sage
story.text: A powerful king named Vishvamitra tried to take a holy cow from a sage by force, and lost, badly, to a man with no army at all. Stung, he gave up his kingdom and spent years in practice, failing and starting again, until even the sage he'd fought called him a great sage. Tradition says he's the one who first heard the Gayatri.
story.source: the Ramayana's telling of Vishvamitra (Bala Kanda); tradition names him the Gayatri's seer
